title: Slides and Visuals
summary: Make slides that support a talk: one idea each, headlines that state the message, simple charts and useful speaker notes.
objectives: Write a slide headline that states the message.
Choose a simple chart and remove clutter.
Move detail from slides into speaker notes.

explanation.heading: Slides support the speaker
explanation.body: Slides are not your script or your handout. They are visual support for what you say. If the audience can read the slide faster than you can speak, they stop listening to you. A good slide is understood in about three seconds, leaving attention for your voice. Aim for large text, few words and one clear picture. A useful check is the 3-second test: show the slide to a friend for three seconds, hide it and ask what the point was. If they cannot say, the slide is doing too much. Also remember that colour, contrast and font size matter in a real room: projectors wash out light colours and the back row sees small text as noise.

explanation.heading: One idea per slide, with a message headline
explanation.body: Each slide should carry **one idea**. If you need the word "and" in the headline, consider two slides. Replace topic labels with **message headlines**: instead of "Sales" write "Sales doubled after the app launch". A reader who reads only the headlines in order should understand your whole argument. Keep headlines to one or two lines and below, supporting content: one image, chart or three short points at most. For a ten-minute talk, six to ten slides are usually plenty. If your deck has thirty slides, you probably have thirty ideas, and the audience will remember none of them.

explanation.heading: Simple charts
explanation.body: Choose the chart for the question. **Line** charts show change over time. **Bar** charts compare categories. A **table** is good for exact values. Avoid 3-D effects, pie charts with many slices and decoration. Remove gridlines, extra colours and legends where labels can sit directly on the data. Use one highlight colour for the point you want noticed and grey for the rest. Always label axes with units, and start bar charts at zero so that sizes are not exaggerated.

explanation.heading: Speaker notes and text walls
explanation.body: A **text wall** is a slide of full sentences. Move detail into **speaker notes** or a separate handout. Notes should hold your key phrases, numbers, transitions to the next slide and timing marks, not a script to read aloud. For code or technical diagrams, show only the lines or boxes that matter and highlight them. Check readability by viewing the slide from the back of the room or at small size: if you cannot read it, resize it. Use consistent fonts and spacing so the design stays out of the way. Pick one or two fonts, one main colour and one accent colour for the whole deck. Align items to a grid and leave empty space; white space is not wasted, it directs attention. Finally, always test the file on the actual projector or screen share before the session.

examples.title: Headline rewrite
examples.body: Before: "Project Update". After: "We will launch two weeks early if testing finishes by Friday". The second tells the audience what to remember.
examples.takeaway: A headline should be a message, not a label.

examples.title: Clutter removed
examples.body: Arun's chart had five colours, a legend, gridlines and a 3-D effect. He kept one line in blue, labelled the end value and greyed the rest. The trend became obvious in three seconds.
examples.takeaway: Simplify and highlight the one thing that matters.

options: Support tickets fell 30% after the new FAQ
exercises.why: It makes a specific claim the slide proves.

exercises.prompt: A ____ chart is best for showing change over time. (one word)
exercises.why: Line charts show trends over time.

exercises.prompt: A slide has a paragraph of text about why you chose Node.js for a project. Rewrite it as one slide: write the headline, what visual or three short points go on the slide, and what goes into the speaker notes.

descriptors.3: One visual or three short points.

exercises.modelAnswer: Headline: "Node.js let us ship the API in two weeks". Slide: three points with icons: one language for front and back end, large package library, fast to prototype. Notes: mention the team already knew JavaScript, the 120-package ecosystem we used, and the two-week delivery date; transition to the testing slide.
exercises.guidance: Good rewrites turn a label into a message, keep three short points and move detail to notes. Avoid pasting the paragraph into a smaller font.

task.title: Redesign three slides
task.brief: Improve three slides from an old presentation, or create three new ones.
steps: Rewrite each headline as a message.
Cut each slide to one idea and one visual.
Move removed detail to speaker notes.
View each slide at small size to check readability.
checklist: I kept one idea per slide
task.evidencePrompt: Write your three new headlines and what you removed.

quiz.prompt: A good slide is understood in about:
quiz.why: Quick understanding leaves attention for the speaker.
The headlines should carry the argument.

quiz.prompt: Bar charts should usually start at:
Detail removed from a slide belongs in the speaker ____. (one word)
quiz.why: Notes hold detail so slides stay clear.

bank.prompt: A slide full of sentences is called:
bank.why: Text walls make audiences read instead of listen.

bank.prompt: To direct attention in a chart use:
options: One highlight colour with grey for the rest
bank.why: A single highlight draws the eye.

cards.back: One idea, one visual, large text, understood in three seconds.
Reading only the headlines should give the whole argument.
Line for time, bar for categories, table for exact values; label axes and highlight one thing.
Key phrases, numbers, transitions and timing, not a script.

reflection: Look at your last presentation. Which slide would you cut or split first, and why?

keyPoints: Charts should be simple and labelled.
revision.redo: Reduce one text-heavy slide to a headline and one visual.
